organization_description: The Unjournal commissions rigorous, public peer evaluation of quantitative research — especially in economics, policy, and social science — that informs global priorities and the most effective interventions for improving lives. description: The Unjournal is running a Fermi (aka BOTEC) modeling hack/workshop on the cost of producing cultivated meat. This follows our researcher/practitioner workshop and PQ work generating an initial public Monte Carlo model/calculator , public discussion, and belief elicitation and synthesis (preliminary version here ). A rough plan for the hack is sketched here . Looking for feedback and suggestions on this. This could also serve as a model for future workshops in other contexts. It should also offer some insight into the reliability of these modeling approaches in general. I’ve often wondered: these models seem to often depend on a lot of structural and definitional assumptions. How sensitive are they to reasonable initial choices? To what extent would independent groups engaging in these BOTECs tend to converge? We’re looking for a modeling co-coordinator and co-facilitator as a one-off role, but it may lead to more such work depending on success and funding. You’d likely work with David Reinstein, David Manheim, and workshop participants in prepping, running, and following this up. We can offer only modest compensation (perhaps up to $1,000 delivered as a Tremendous reward for at least 20 hours of work). The Workshop Aims to Do a Combination of Provide a clearly-explained workspace, with common estimands and parameter definitions, aligning understanding, terminology, etc. Further consolidate and refine sourced beliefs and evidence, identifying remaining uncertainty and high-value next steps. Enable and encourage workshop participants (at least a few individuals or groups) to model this independently, considering convergence, reliability, and modeling degrees of freedom (and providing insights for future modeling approaches and workshops in general). Build, improve, and communicate a reasoning-transparent “consensus model.” If you’re the co-coordinator, you could support us in planning and preparing for the hack, coordinating and running it, and following up, analyzing, and communicating the results. It could be tied to a formal/academic research project if it makes sense for you. The co-coordinator should have hands-on experience building, auditing, or seriously assessing quantitative models. Relevant backgrounds include probabilistic or Monte Carlo modeling, forecasting, cost-effectiveness analysis, techno-economic analysis, Squiggle, or something similar. Experience coordinating collaborative workshops and familiarity with cultivated meat would also be useful. General facilitation or operations experience alone isn’t enough for this role. If applicants have a relevant model, analysis, code repository, or other work sample, we would be glad to see it, but it is not required. If interested, please email contact@unjournal.org as soon as you can (ideally before 24 September 2026) to express your interest and share your CV/work samples/experience. Also looking for referrals/nominations. And feel free to ask questions or “apply in the comments” if you want to do this publicly.

title: Legal Advisor
organization_description: Asia Accountability Initiative (AAI) works with local advocates to hold companies to their animal welfare commitments across Asia. Hundreds of hotel, food and restaurant companies have publicly pledged to use only cage-free eggs. Many are behind or have quietly excluded Asian markets, and we help hold them to account.
description: We’re building a small network of lawyers across Asia who will help us campaign boldly and lawfully. This is not a staff position: you advise on specific requests as they come up, either pro bono or paid by the hour . We’re looking for advisors in mainland China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam . Work is remote. About Asia Accountability Initiative Asia Accountability Initiative (AAI) works with local advocates to hold companies to their animal welfare commitments across Asia. Hundreds of hotel, food and restaurant companies have publicly pledged to use only cage-free eggs. Many are behind or have quietly excluded Asian markets, and we help hold them to account. We closely support six country accountability initiatives, in China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia. Most of our work focuses on cage-free egg commitments: making sure companies deliver what they have promised. Our work combines direct engagement with companies, public campaigns, media work and a network of more than 5,000 digital volunteers. In mainland China we don’t run traditional public pressure campaigns. We look for creative approaches that fit the local context, and we need advice that is realistic about what is possible there. Why Work With Us A few hours of your time can help change how millions of animals live. Impact at scale. Asia produces more than half of the world’s eggs, and most hens here are still confined in battery cages. When a multinational keeps its cage-free promise, the change reaches every farm in its supply chain across the region. High leverage. Good legal advice is often the difference between a campaign that launches and one that stays on the shelf. A short review from you can unlock months of our team’s work. A gap only you can fill. Very few lawyers in the region advise animal advocates. Your expertise would go where it is scarce and needed. Interesting work. Questions sit where media, consumer, NGO and corporate law meet, often with no clear precedent. Recognition and community. With your permission, we’ll credit you or your firm as a pro bono partner, and connect you with the wider animal advocacy movement in Asia. How We Think About Legal Risk We want an advisor who helps us find a lawful way to do something, not just reasons not to do it. Campaigning for corporate accountability carries some legal risk by nature. We name companies publicly, criticise their track record, and ask the public to act. We accept reasonable, well-understood risk to make progress for animals. What doesn’t work for us is advice that rejects anything with any risk at all. For each request, we’d ask you to tell us: How risky it is (low, medium or high) and why. The realistic worst case and how likely it is, for example a demand letter, a lawsuit, or a regulator or police response. What changes would lower the risk while keeping the message intact. We make the final decision on what risk to take, informed by your advice. What You’d Do Review campaign materials before release: press releases, campaign webpages, social media posts, ads, petitions and video scripts. You’d flag issues such as defamation, use of company names and logos, parody, and claims we need to be able to prove. Give general guidance on what is and isn’t allowed in your jurisdiction, including protests and public stunts, permits, volunteer activities, and collecting supporter data through petitions and sign-ups. Help us respond when a company pushes back, for example a letter from their lawyers, and tell us when we need formal representation. In future, advise on registering a local nonprofit entity, including rules on NGO registration and foreign funding. Materials are usually in the local language. We’d like your advice in English. Who We’re Looking For We welcome applications from individual lawyers, law firms and their pro bono teams, and legal clinics or legal NGOs. You should have: A licence to practise in one of the jurisdictions above (for firms and clinics, qualified lawyers who would do the work). Experience in at least one of: media and defamation, advertising or intellectual property, NGO and civil society law, public assembly or human rights, or corporate law. A belief that civil society has a legitimate role in holding companies to account. The ability to give clear, practical written advice in English, quickly. No conflict of interest with the companies we campaign on (mostly large hotel, food and restaurant groups), or a willingness to tell us upfront. It’s a plus if you have: Experience advising NGOs, journalists, activists or campaign groups. An interest in animal welfare or food systems. You don’t need to be an animal advocate, but you do need to be comfortable with our mission.

In This Role, You Will Be Expected To… Develop research projects to identify high-impact, cost-effective interventions for improving fish welfare in Ghana. Improve the quality and reliability of field data, including collection protocols. Monitor and evaluate the data from the projects, and regularly update management. title: Research Program Lead
organization_description: Animal Welfare League is a nonprofit working with corporate companies to improve farmed-animal welfare across Africa. We secure corporate policies through research, negotiation, peaceful public actions, and strategic media.
description: The Animal Welfare League is commissioning its first substantial body of independent research: three studies across South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt on the economics of cage-free egg production, the spread of cage systems in broiler production, and the real cost of building aviary laying hen housing in African conditions. We’re looking for someone to lead this program. This is a commissioning and quality role , not one that involves writing the research itself. You will define what gets studied, select who studies it, hold them to a rigorous standard, and ensure the results meet the expectations of the institutions, regulators, and companies whose decisions they’re meant to inform. The program is deliberately open: every study we commission is published in full, whatever the outcome, under an open license, with its underlying data. You would be responsible for protecting that openness under pressure. Primary Responsibilities Program management. Run the three 2026–27 studies on time and according to budget. Maintain the schedule against the external deadlines that matter, particularly standard processes, and proactively communicate when a deadline or deliverable is at risk. Commissioning. Draft terms of reference and calls for proposals. Run open calls and invited procurements. Assemble and service evaluation panels. Negotiate and manage contracts, milestones and payments with researchers and institutions. Research quality. Interrogate proposed methods before committing money. Ensure that protocols are pre-registered where appropriate, that assumptions are published, and that comparability is maintained where several pieces of work must be read together. Catch weak analysis before it’s published, not after. Partnerships. Work with civil society partners, academic institutions and consultants across the continent, including our collaboration with Animal Law Reform South Africa. Represent AWL in technical and standards settings when possible. Use and dissemination. Turn commissioned research and policy work into submissions, policy briefs and materials that decision-makers actually read. Track where the evidence lands and what it changes. Funding. Support applications to co-fund the program, working with the Executive Director. Our current research budget is modest, and part of this role is making it go further. Required Qualifications The ability to read a quantitative analysis or an economic model and judge whether it is sound. This is the core of the role. Experience commissioning, managing or supervising research in a non-profit, academic, government or consultancy setting. A postgraduate qualification in agricultural or applied economics, animal science, public policy, statistics or a related field, or equivalent practical experience. Written English to publication standard. Sound judgment about evidence, including the confidence to tell a funder, a partner or your own organization that a finding does not hold. Experience developing policy positions or engaging legislative, regulatory or institutional processes. Willingness to build a body of work in an area where little exists and to start by establishing the facts rather than by arguing a position. Comfort working remotely, independently and across time zones. Preferred Candidates Experience in African agriculture or the poultry sector. Familiarity with the Three Rs framework (Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement), animal research ethics, or institutional ethics review. Knowledge in legislative drafting, model provisions or regulatory submissions. Familiarity with standards-development processes, whether national, regional or international. Experience in research procurement, contracting or grant management. A record of published or commissioned work. Familiarity with the Open Wing Alliance or the farmed animal welfare movement. Fluency in French or Arabic. What We Offer A program with real independence written into its terms, and an organization that will back you when a finding is inconvenient. Direct influence over what gets researched on farm animal welfare in Africa, at a point when very little of it exists. The chance to build AWL’s work on animals used in research from the beginning, and to shape its direction. Flexible hours and full remote working. Named credit on the programme’s published outputs.

title: Grantmaker-In-Residence
organization_description: We prioritise our projects based on their estimated impact on the world. Our longer projects tend to be with clients giving tens of millions or more a year and making significant changes to their giving. However, we are pretty open to having quick advising calls with philanthropists of any size. We typically have more project opportunities than capacity, so in some cases our highest value-add may be connecting you to other actors. Each year, Elevate offers a limited number of pro bono engagements particularly focused on new and early first-time donors.
description: Over the course of a year, the Fieldshaper program develops you into a field-leading grantmaker. You’ll steward $1,000,000 in grant capital, receive a $125,000 annual stipend, and deploy that capital within a sub-field of one of three key areas (farmed animals, global health, or philanthropic infrastructure); building the track record to become a grantmaker who can shape a field. Role Details Title: Grantmaker-in-Residence (Leader of the X fund or Grantmaker in Y area also possible options) Location: Hybrid: remote with four mandatory in-person weeks (London; New York; San Francisco; a cause-track conference in London, Oxford, or Mexico depending on cause area) Compensation: A living stipend of ~$125,000 for the year Duration: 12 months, full-time, February 2027 – January 2028 Focus areas: Farmed animal welfare, philanthropic infrastructure, global health, global aid policy Goal: To create the next generation of fieldshapers and active grantmakers How to apply: Fill out this form (by October 30th) Program The Elevate Philanthropy fieldshaper program is a one-year training program that turns generalist, high-agency professionals into active grantmakers and general managers of problems. After 6 weeks of intensive training, each resident will deploy $1,000,000 of grant capital across the rest of the year, similar to a program officer role at a foundation or the leader of a philanthropic fund. The program aims to create a pathway into philanthropy and to develop the next generation of grantmakers, with an emphasis on active deployment and ecosystem thinking. An active grantmaker sources and builds funding opportunities, rather than passively processing grant requests, and a fieldshaper owns an entire problem and aims to do whatever it takes to solve it. Developed by the co-founder of Ambitious Impact’s Charity Entrepreneurship program, an incubator behind 50+ high-impact charities, the program will train grantmakers who grow and affect the broader field they operate in. Residents join one of three cause tracks (Animal Welfare, Global Health, or Philanthropic Infrastructure) and complete a six-week bootcamp before deploying capital into a specific sub-area within their chosen track (e.g. effective careers, or fish welfare in Asia). After this, five months of weekly structured sessions will run alongside live grantmaking. In the second half of the year, this tapers to weekly coaching as residents scale their deployment. The program includes four in-person weeks: kick-off in London; one each at conferences in San Francisco and New York, and one at a cause-relevant conference (the AVA Summit or EAG London). These give fieldshapers time to get to know one another and to meet other grantmakers, funders, and actors in their field. The year closes with a published piece of thought leadership, a one-year grant portfolio, and a demo-day-style event where residents present how they deployed their funding. Each pool is structured as a fund, with ongoing opportunities (though not guarantees) for top-ups and increased funding volume. What You Will Do The key goal is to deploy $1,000,000 in grant capital over the year impactfully. Deploy this capital in a way that builds up the specific sub-field your granting is in, and in a way that is cost-effective in terms of the amount of good done per $. Deploy the majority of capital actively, e.g. creating opportunities or finding funding options that other grantmakers would miss. Build a pipeline of ~20 funding opportunities in your cause track, run due diligence scaled to grant size, and make the case for or against funding to a review process. Long-term, you will also consider assessing grant opportunities beyond single organizations; looking at fund managers and pooled vehicles, as well as actively co-building new projects in the field. As you demonstrate your grantmaking ability, you will build out your portfolio and potentially fundraise with your new funder network, to further develop the area. What You Will Learn There is some basic learning about how to be a grantmaker (e.g. areas covered in this book ), but the program is primarily focused on building active grantmaking and fieldshaping tools. This is broken down into 4 subsections: Ecosystem-level thinking: For example, being able to analyze an area and determine where a marginal funder should deploy more capital to increase the total impact in the field. Creating opportunities: For example, finding talented individuals and providing them with the necessary capital and support to advance an intervention in an area that would have not otherwise progressed. Complex judgment: For example, being able to weigh factors like the talent counterfactuals of a grant, and how a given project connects to the broader ecosystem. Coordination: For example, if it makes sense to build up a donor collaboration in your area, and if so, which actors would be best positioned to join it. What You Leave With A full year’s grantmaking track record, $1,000,000 deployed, a clear explanation for your theory of change for your field improving, published thought leadership under your name, introductions to grantmaking organisations, and working relationships with other highly talented fieldshapers you’ve learned and worked alongside. We think anyone who goes through the program will be in a good place to be hired by existing and new foundations, launch their own fund, or kick off a career in active grantmaking in general. The reason we are running this program is that we believe there is a shortage of great grantmakers relative to funding and the hiring needs of growing foundations. Currently, there is no clear pathway for someone to get started into the field, and we see this long-term career impact as the primary driver of this program’s impact. What We Are Looking For Traits: Rigor and intellectual honesty under ambiguity; decision-making grounded in evidence. Clear decision-making grounded in evidence and logic. Comfort with the responsibility of directing large amounts of capital. Ability to do high-quality self-directed work and gain knowledge quickly in a field. No prior grantmaking experience required (we are equally excited about applicants who have none). Example Target Demographics Mid-career Professionals Profile: Mid-career, currently in an adjacent sector (consulting, entrepreneurship, tech, policy) and looking for a structured route into philanthropy. This program appeals because it compresses the learning of years of on-the-job grantmaking into twelve months, backed by capital and warm introductions to grantmakers. Concrete example: An ex-consultant who did three years of consulting and then founded her own firm. She is exceptional at the work and disappointed by its lack of impact. She has been filling evenings and weekends with volunteering and reading about social issues online. She has not picked a cause area and grantmaking feels like the best nonprofit role that would check boxes she has in terms of risk, intellectual challenge, and impact at the same time. However, the path to get there is completely unclear. Nonprofit Founders and Operators Profile: People who have founded, run, or held senior operating roles at high-impact, evidence-based nonprofits and now want to move to the funding side. They arrive with grantee-side experience and a working knowledge of what organizations need from funders, which gives them an advantage in matching funders to the right grantees. Example: A founder who spent seven years building an NGO. He wants more leverage than a single organisation can offer and has a deep sense of how the ecosystem he operates in works. Philanthropic Actors Without Fieldshaping Experience Profile: People who have done grantmaking or philanthropic advisory before and are looking to increase their ability to do active grantmaking and more intentional fieldshaping. Example: Someone who currently works at a classic foundation, but has found that even actors at the top of their field leave a lot of gaps in the ecosystem that are hard to fill, despite significant capital to deploy. They want their next grantmaking role to be more directly connected to building up the field. Recruitment Process The recruitment vetting is an intense process, but we aim to make each of the steps useful for the candidates in assessing their fit with grantmaking as a career path. Applications are open now, and close October 30th. We aim to have acceptance offers out to candidates by mid-December, with the program starting in February. title: Global Growth Manager/Lead
organization_description: Fish Welfare Initiative (FWI) is a relatively new, ACE-recommended organization whose mission is to improve the welfare of fishes as much as possible. We focus specifically on farmed fishes, or fishes raised in aquaculture. Our main country of implementation is India, where we currently work in the Nellore and West Godavari districts. ​ As part of our Alliance for Responsible Aquaculture (ARA), we work with over 100 fish farms. Through this program, we estimate that we have already improved the lives of over one million fishes, though we intend to have a much greater impact in the coming years. Learn more about our plans and our organization in our blog.
description: Fish Welfare Initiative (FWI) is hiring a Global Growth Manager or Lead to scope and identify the next country(ies) for FWI’s international expansion. We are seeking someone for this role who is experienced working internationally, skilled at both desk research and scoping visits, and comfortable with significant time traveling. If you are excited to work autonomously, prioritize strategically, and be FWI’s first “boots on the ground”, this might be the right role for you. Before reading further, please note: The only prior experience strictly required is that you have spent extended time traveling or living independently in countries unfamiliar to you. See more below. People of any nationality may apply. You will be expected to spend six months or more in-country (likely various countries in Asia) during the first one to two years of the role. Afterwards, more of the work can be done remotely. Apply with our initial mini test task, linked below, by Sunday, September 20. About Fish Welfare Initiative (FWI) Fish Welfare Initiative is an animal welfare organization that focuses on one of the most numerous and neglected groups of farmed animals: fishes. We work to improve farmed fish welfare by developing and implementing scalable, cost-effective, and evidence-based interventions. Our core program, the Alliance for Responsible Aquaculture (ARA), partners with fish farmers in Andhra Pradesh, India to improve water quality and reduce stocking densities. Our Research & Development (R&D) department designs and tests new interventions that can become future programs. Our prior work has focused primarily on India and China. Your task will be to identify and support early-stage work in our next country. You can learn more about our work on our blog and website.​ Key Responsibilities The following are the key responsibilities you would have: Desk research: Conduct extensive desk research to inform which countries to visit. This will include weighted factor models and expert interviews. Field visits: Conduct extensive scoping visits to prioritized countries. Field visits will involve farm visits, stakeholder visits, and developing a general understanding of what it would be like to work in this country. You will likely be given a budget to hire in-country contractors to support this work. For an example of the sort of reports you will complete, see our scoping reports from Vietnam and the Philippines (also note that, particularly in the case of our Vietnam report, our quality standards have since improved). Recommendation and report writing: Based on your desk and field research, submit a report to the Executive Director regarding which country(ies) FWI should expand to. Early stage operations: Support or lead the early-stage operations in our next country of focus. This likely includes hiring, management, strategy, and legal support. Requirements Required Criteria International experience: You have spent extended time—three months or more, cumulatively—traveling, living, or working independently outside your home country, including in lower-income countries and outside of major cities. This need not have been across many countries; sustained time in one unfamiliar country can count. Skills: You are extremely organized, able to work autonomously, and comfortable making high-level decisions under conditions of extreme uncertainty. Values: You believe in the importance of fish welfare, and/or are aligned with the values of effective altruism. Ideal Criteria You have previously conducted country scoping and prioritization work. You have worked previously in the animal advocacy or effective altruism spaces. You have previous knowledge of or experience with aquaculture. Designation and Reporting We are considering two different designations for this role: Global Growth Manager: More junior, likely for applicants with 5 or less years of work experience. Global Growth Lead: More senior. You will be expected to work more autonomously, and likely will own more of the early-stage in-country operations (for instance, by having initial local staff reporting to you). We expect this role to report to the Executive Director. That may change, however, if we hire multiple staff at different seniority levels for this role. The Fine Print Location: You should expect to work six months or more in-country during the first one to two years (cumulative, not continuous). After that, more flexibility will be given to work remotely. Position-Status: Full-time, permanent. Start Date: ASAP, with some flexibility. Salary Range: Flexible. We have a wide budget of $25K to $70K for this role, depending on the applicant’s needs (e.g., location/cost of living). Benefits: Generous paid time off (up to 40 days of personal leave), parental leave, flexible hours, and the opportunity to work for a cause you believe in.​ How to Apply Please complete our mini test task. It should take about 1.5 hours total (excluding any time to prepare your CV). FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS Which countries are you considering scoping? Given a) numbers of fishes farmed, and b) our prior work experience, we are most interested in countries in South or Southeast Asia. Countries we are excited about now include the Philippines, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, etc. We will likely ask you to investigate these countries first. We are open to considering other countries, and possibly open to considering other regions, based on your initial research. What will the hiring process be like? We will share the full hiring process with all candidates who pass round one. You can roughly expect the following stages: Mini test task (~1.5 hours) Full application form (~1.5 hours) Asynchronous Interview (~30 minutes) Interview (~1 hour) In-Person Paid Work Trial (1-2 days, also with travel) Candidates will be eliminated at each stage. You will be notified at each stage how many applicants remain, so that you might better understand your odds of acceptance. Where can/should I be based out of when I’m not traveling for this role? That’s largely up to you, though we do have some preferences (though these are not hard criteria): It is challenging to have staff based in the Americas, due to timezone differences and travel costs to Asia. You would benefit from living at our headquarters in Eluru, Andhra Pradesh, India, as this is where a large portion of our team is based. You would also benefit from living in South or Southeast Asia, either in one of the countries we might scope or in a regional hub (e.g. Singapore). I think I would be a great fit, but I can’t travel 6 or more cumulative months in a year. Should I still apply? No, this is a hard requirement. What will success in Year 1 look like? A successful first year may look like you having: Conducted prioritization research on a larger number of countries. Conducted scoping visits in a couple of the most promising countries. Recommended to the team an initial country to expand to. Supported the early operations in that country, such as the hiring of local staff. Will I be considered for the Manager or Lead designation? See above for the distinction. This is a single hiring process for both designations, and we will decide which one makes sense for you to be considered for in the later stages of the process. How many staff will you hire for this role? For this position, if we find multiple strong applicants, it is possible we will hire more than one. We are interested in investing heavily in determining the right country, or countries, to expand to. Why such a large salary range? This is because we are open to a variety of experience levels and people with different costs of living. This is a key role for our organization, and we are willing to pay what is needed to get the right person. Do I need to speak any specific language (besides English), or have prior knowledge of farmed fishes? No, neither of these is strictly necessary, though prior knowledge of farmed fishes will be helpful. Likewise, speaking a language in a country we may scope will be helpful. Do I have to have previous animal advocacy experience in order to be eligible for this role? No. Previous animal advocacy experience is helpful but not required. We are, however, seeking someone who is deeply committed to improving the lives of animals. Will FWI support visas and travel? Yes, including relocation and housing support. We’ll work out specifics with the right candidate based on their situation. What is it like to work at FWI? See our blog for our recent culture surveys with unfiltered answers from our team.
